s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Sexual Misbehavior
s.d: sexual intercourse of a man with a married woman other than his own spouse
s.c: From the standpoint of the NT, adultery was normally defined in terms of the married status of the woman involved in any such act. In other words, sexual intercourse of a married man with an unmarried woman would usually be regarded as πορνεία ‘fornication’ (LN 88.271), but sexual intercourse of either an unmarried or a married man with someone else’s wife was regarded as adultery, both on the part of the man as well as the woman. In view of the married status of the woman being the determining factor in μοιχάω, μοιχεύω, μοιχάομαι, μοιχεία, and related terms (LN 88.277-LN 88.278), there is a significant contrast with πορνεύω and related expressions (LN 88.271). πορνεύω, however, may be regarded as more generic in meaning, and thus in certain contexts including adultery.|⟦Matthew 5:32|Matthew 5:32⟧ is usually rendered as ‘anyone who divorces his wife for any cause other than fornication makes her guilty of committing adultery,’ presumably on the implication that she would marry someone else, as is implied in the final clause of the verse.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: the soft material that fills the cavity in the bones
s.c: There are certain problems, however, involved in the rendering of ⟦Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12⟧, for strictly speaking there is no one point at which joints and marrow may be separated. Similarly, the expression ‘to where joints and marrow come together’ seems rather anomalous, since the joints bring together various bones, but they are not joined together with marrow. This passage in ⟦Hebrews 4:12|Hebrews 4:12⟧ is essentially figurative in that it is speaking of the word of God being sharper than a two-edged sword cutting all the way through to where soul and spirit meet, and this is described as being parallel to where joints and marrow come together. Perhaps one can best state this in some languages as ‘to where the joints and the marrow are,’ thus suggesting that part of the human body farthest from the surface.

s.dp: Constructions › Miscellaneous Constructions
s.d: a construction of two flat stones between which grain was ground into flour by rotating the top stone
s.c: Some mills were relatively small and operated by hand and could well be considered as artifacts. Others, however, were quite large, and animals were used to rotate the upper stone.|In almost all parts of the world grain is ground in one way or another. Quite frequently mills are of the same general structure as those used in ancient times, in which two relatively large, round, flat stones were placed one on top of the other, and the grain was ground between the two stones. Grain entered the mill through a round hole in the upper stone, and the flour gradually emerged from around the edges of the two stones. In other parts of the world, however, grain is prepared by means of grinding stones called metates. In still other parts of the world, a mortar and pestle are used for the grinding or preparation of grain. In most contexts, what is important is either the large size of the stones or the function of grinding grain, not necessarily the particular form. However, in contexts which speak about tying a millstone to a man’s neck (see LN 7.69) and his being thrown into the depths of the sea, it is important to refer to relatively large stones which would cause a person to sink immediately. In such a context the use of a term for ‘mortar,’ especially one of wood, would hardly be appropriate since it would normally float. Frequently μύλος may be rendered as ‘stones for grinding grain.’ In other instances, even a more generic expression may be used, for example, ‘a large stone.’

s.dp: Constructions › Miscellaneous Constructions

s.c: μύλος ‘mill’ (LN 7.68) denotes a mill as a whole, while μύλος denotes only one of the large flat stones of a mill. For a discussion of some of the translational problems involved in rendering μύλος ‘millstone,’ see the discussion on μύλος (LN 7.68).

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (causative derivative of {L:μωρία<SDBG:μωρία:000000>} ‘foolishness,’ {D:32.57}) to cause the content of certain thoughts to become devoid of meaning
s.c: In ⟦1 Corinthians 1:20|1 Corinthians 1:20⟧ the focus is upon the content of wisdom and nonsense, and it may be necessary to make this explicit, for example, ‘the people of the world thought that what they understood was wise, but God showed that their thoughts were foolish’ or ‘… their way of thinking was foolish.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (derivative of {L:μωρός<SDBG:μωρός:000000>}[a] ‘unwise, foolish,’ {D:32.55}) to become one who does not employ a capacity to understand and thus acts very foolishly
s.g: to become foolish; to act more foolishly

s.dp: Features of Objects › Sweet, Bitter, Tasteless
s.d: to become insipid or tasteless
s.g: to become tasteless; to lose taste
s.c: In ⟦Matthew 5:13|Matthew 5:13⟧ μωραίνομαι is equivalent to ἄναλος (LN 5.27), that is to say, to be without a salt taste. Pure salt cannot actually lose its taste, but the sodium chloride of impure salt can be leached out, especially in humid weather, and the remaining substance is accordingly tasteless. See also discussion at LN 5.25.

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: the content of foolish thought
s.g: foolishness; nonsense; what is thought to be foolish
s.c: In rendering ⟦1 Corinthians 1:18|1 Corinthians 1:18⟧ it is important to recognize that ‘foolishness’ must be defined in terms of the relationship that it has to those who ‘are being destroyed.’ Therefore, it may be important to translate ⟦1 Corinthians 1:18|1 Corinthians 1:18⟧ as ‘those who are being destroyed think that the message concerning the cross is nonsense’ or ‘… makes no sense’ or ‘… simply cannot be understood.’

s.dp: Communication › Foolish Talk
s.d: talk which is both foolish and stupid

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: pertaining to being extremely unwise and foolish
s.c: In rendering μωρός in ⟦1 Corinthians 4:10|1 Corinthians 4:10⟧ it is essential to recognize the rhetorical exaggeration. Paul is not stating that he and his colleagues actually act unwisely or foolishly, and so it may be necessary in some languages to translate ‘we are fools for Christ’s sake’ as ‘we are regarded as fools for Christ’s sake’ or ‘it might seem that we are fools in order to serve Christ.’

s.dp: Understand › Lack of Capacity for Understanding
s.d: (derivative of {L:μωρία<SDBG:μωρία:000000>} ‘foolishness,’ {D:32.57}) pertaining to thoughts devoid of understanding and therefore foolish
s.c: Some translators have endeavored to render μωρός in the sense of 'nonsense´ as 'that which cannot be understood,´ but this could refer to some type of deep mystery. Accordingly, the expression 'what the world considered to be nonsense´ can often be better rendered as ‘what the world thinks makes no sense’ or ‘what so many people think is foolishness.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: the leader of the Israelites out of Egypt and the lawgiver

s.dp: Communication › Written Language
s.d: the Law given through Moses, as formulated in the first five books of the OT
s.g: the Law; the Law of Moses; the Law given through Moses; Moses
s.c: In a number of languages it is quite appropriate to refer to the writings of a person by simply mentioning the author, but in many languages this cannot be done. Furthermore, in ⟦2 Corinthians 3:15|2 Corinthians 3:15⟧ it may be necessary to employ an active expression, so that one must translate ‘whenever people read the laws which God gave through Moses.’ The use of Μωϋσῆς as a reference to the Law of Moses also occurs in the phrase ‘Moses and the prophets’ as a reference to the sacred writings (compare ὁ νόμος καὶ οἱ προφῆται ‘the sacred writings,’ LN 33.58).

s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a town in the south central part of Galilee

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Ναζαρέθ ‘Nazareth,’ {D:93.536}) a person who lives in or is a native of Nazareth
s.c: Ναζορηνός, Ναζωρηνός, and Ναζωρινός (⟦Mark 10:47|Mark 10:47⟧, apparatus) are incidental alternative spellings.

s.d: an alternative form of {L:Ναζαρηνός<SDBG:Ναζαρηνός:000000>}, {D:93.537} ({S:04000202300032 04201803700014})

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a disciple of Jesus

s.dp: Affirmation, Negation › Affirmation
s.d: an affirmative response to questions or statements or an emphatic affirmation of a statement
s.g: yes; yes it is true that; yes it is so; sure; indeed

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a Syrian army commander healed by Elisha

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in southern Galilee

s.dp: Constructions › Buildings
s.d: a building in which a deity is worshiped (in the case of the Temple in Jerusalem, a place where God was also regarded as dwelling)
s.c: ναός may often be rendered as ‘the house of God’ or ‘the place where God dwells’ or ‘God’s building.’ In some languages it is most naturally referred to as ‘the holy house’ or ‘the holy place.’ See also LN 7.16.|ναός is used figuratively in ⟦John 2:21|John 2:21⟧ (ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔλεγεν περὶ τοῦ ναοῦ τοῦ σώματος αὐτοῦ ‘but he spoke of the temple of his body’ or ‘… of his body as a temple’) and in ⟦1 Corinthians 6:19|1 Corinthians 6:19⟧, where the believer’s body is spoken of as ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματος ‘the temple of the Holy Spirit within you.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Images and Idols
s.d: a small replica or model of a temple or shrine{N:001}
s.g: replica temple; model of a shrine
s.c: In ⟦Acts 19:24|Acts 19:24⟧ the term ναός refers only to a small replica of the temple of Artemis. An equivalent of ναός in ⟦Acts 19:24|Acts 19:24⟧ is in some languages ‘tiny temples of Artemis,’ or, in other instances, it is ‘souvenir temples of Artemis.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Artifacts › Perfumes and Incense
s.d: an aromatic oil extracted from a plant called nard
s.g: oil of nard; perfume of nard
s.c: Translators normally borrow the term ‘nard’ but employ some type of classifier, for example, ‘a perfume called nard’ or ‘a sweet-smelling substance, nard.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person whose household is greeted in {S:04501601100020}

s.dp: Maritime Activities
s.d: to experience or suffer shipwreck
s.c: In some languages it is necessary to specify the particular cause of a shipwreck, for example, ‘the ship struck a rock or reef’ or ‘the ship sank because of a storm’ or ‘the ship collided with another ship and sank.’ In view of the context of ⟦2 Corinthians 11:25|2 Corinthians 11:25⟧, it is probably best to select an expression which would refer to a ship sinking because of a storm, though obviously one cannot be certain.

s.dp: Maritime Activities
s.d: one who owns a ship
s.c: For an illustrative example, see ⟦Acts 27:11|Acts 27:11⟧ in LN 54.28.

s.dp: Artifacts › Boats and Parts of Boats
s.d: a larger ocean-going vessel used for transporting cargo and people
s.c: The term ναῦς occurs in the NT only in ⟦Acts 27:41|Acts 27:41⟧, where it refers to the ship which was wrecked at Malta. See LN 6.42.

s.dp: Maritime Activities
s.d: one who works on a ship
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of ναύτης is ‘one who handles the ropes’ or ‘one who works on a boat.’

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Persons
s.d: a person in the genealogy of Jesus

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the harbor of Philippi in Macedonia

s.dp: People › Males
s.d: a young man beyond the age of puberty, but normally before marriage
s.c: The person referred to as a νεανίας in ⟦Acts 20:9|Acts 20:9⟧ is called a παῖς ‘boy’ (see LN 9.41) in ⟦Acts 20:12|Acts 20:12⟧. This should not be understood as identity in meaning, since the person concerned could have been of such an age that either ‘young man’ or ‘boy’ was a possible denotation. In other words, the age reference of νεανίας and παῖς overlaps in Greek. In a number of languages, however, there is a much more specific and clear-cut distinction in age grading.

s.dp: People › Males
s.d: a young man beyond the age of puberty, but normally before marriage

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Live, Die
s.d: pertaining to being dead
s.c: In some languages it may be difficult or even impossible to speak of ‘the body without the spirit,’ for this would be equivalent to the meaning of ‘corpse,’ and obviously a ‘corpse’ is ‘dead.’ It may therefore be necessary to translate this expression in ⟦James 2:26|James 2:26⟧ as ‘if a person does not have a spirit, he is dead.’

s.dp: Value › Useful, Useless
s.d: pertaining to being utterly useless, with the implication of total lack of purport

s.dp: Able, Capable
s.d: pertaining to being unable to respond to any impulse or to perform some function
s.c: Since the reference in ⟦Ephesians 2:5|Ephesians 2:5⟧ (see also ⟦Ephesians 2:1|Ephesians 2:1⟧) is to matters relating to God, one may translate ‘we who were unable to respond to matters relating to God because of our sins …’ or ‘we who were spiritually dead …’

s.dp: Aspect › Cease, Stop
s.d: a figurative extension of meaning of νεκρόω ‘to put to death,’ not occurring in the NT) to cease completely from activity, with the implication of extreme measures taken to guarantee such a cessation{N:001}
s.g: to stop completely; to cease completely
